title: Satisfactory, Satisfaction and POURS
finding: The current POURS guide uses Satisfactory for the additional principle. The Little Book also contains a source titled POUR + S (Satisfaction). This is an observed naming variation; it does not establish that both sources have identical scope.
proposal: Use Satisfactory for the proposed principle and satisfaction for the experience assessment. Preserve historical titles; add scoped explanations rather than silently renaming source passages.

title: Comparable and equivalent experience
finding: The Little Book governance map uses comparable experience. Synchronistic Design explains equivalent experience in terms of preserved meaning and value. Both reject identical interfaces as the objective; their use substantially overlaps.
proposal: Keep both terms and require a stated comparison across outcomes, effort, privacy, availability, control and dignity. Do not invent an absolute universal distinction or replace every occurrence.

usage_evidence.heading: 2. Shared reasoning foundation
usage_evidence.excerpt: Comparable experience means a fair opportunity to achieve the intended outcome with appropriate quality, control, dignity and effort. It does not require identical interfaces, techniques or completion times. Disabled people's participation supplies knowledge and challenge; agent-generated personas or simulated users cannot replace it.

title: Feelings as research lenses rather than assigned outcomes
finding: The current POURS guide retains the five emotional descriptions and explicitly qualifies them as intended qualities rather than feelings assigned to all users. Older essay wording uses stronger universal language.
proposal: Retain all five labels. Carry the current qualifications whenever summarising the emotional lens; do not interpret historical rhetoric as measured evidence.

title: ACT rules, ACT-style procedures and user scripts
finding: QA supplies a locally structured ACT-style test system, while programme guidance calls for user ACT-style scripts. The W3C ACT work has its own rules format and rule status. These labels must not imply equal scope or external approval.
proposal: Use W3C ACT when that is the actual reference, ACT-style procedural test for local structured procedures, and user-oriented task script for the relevant complete activity. Check existing labels in their own contexts before migration.

title: Robustness, reliability and Feeling Safe
finding: The AI Act delivery guide explicitly distinguishes AI Act robustness from WCAG robustness. POURS uses Feeling Safe as an emotional lens with a separate warning that reassurance does not establish security.
proposal: Adopt the owner-supplied Agentic Robustness definition as a distinct Double-FW definition, retaining WCAG robustness as its separate source-owned term.

usage_evidence.heading: AC06 — Choose methods appropriate to the surface
usage_evidence.excerpt: AI Act robustness and WCAG robustness have related but different meanings. Reliable semantics/accessibility APIs support assistive technologies and some agents. Article 15 addresses accuracy, resilience and cybersecurity. No general requirement to expose an MCP server or unrestricted agent access is asserted.

usage_evidence.excerpt: These are related, but none proves the others. A participant can feel reassured while a security flaw remains. A technically accessible task can still be exhausting. A failed journey can still contain a respectful support interaction. Keep each finding visible.

title: Evidence, status and human authority
finding: The policy guidance separates applicable duties, approved commitments, verified practice and proposals. QA and maturity examples also distinguish actual evidence from prepared or fictional records. Source words such as validated and approved need a stated object and scope.
proposal: Keep observation, estimate, hypothesis, synthetic example, proposal and approval distinct. Preserve unknown, not tested and not applicable as different states. Never infer approval from a template, Git merge or a new export date.

title: Double-FW meanings and externally owned requirements
finding: The POURS guide says its extension does not amend WCAG. The policy repository distinguishes Double-FW secondary guidance from legal-applicability determination. An internal preference cannot silently change an external meaning.
proposal: Use approved Double-FW meanings for Double-FW methodologies, explaining disagreements with external approaches. Preserve source-owned meanings when quoting standards or legal terms. Resolve actual applicability with current primary sources and appropriate expertise.
